entries.title: Hasan Piker Is the New Democratic Litmus Test
entries.summary: Many Democrats aren’t happy about it.
entries.content:
Like late-summer humidity, Hasan Piker hangs heavy over the discourse.

At a rally on Monday, Vice President Vance brought up the hard-left streamer in an attempt to paint the Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed as anti-American. Last week, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries called Piker’s recent statements about Jewish Americans “dangerous and anti-Semitic.” Senators Jon Ossoff, Cory Booker, and Jacky Rosen said much the same. Facing questions about a totally different set of Piker comments, Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez hustled into an elevator.

Some Democrats are trying to dismiss the 35-year-old political commentator as irrelevant. He’s just “a streamer in California,” El-Sayed said on Saturday, waving off questions from reporters. Piker himself has spent the past week casting himself as the victim of hysteria. “I have become this media cycle’s ‘trans athletes’ or ‘migrant caravan,’” he posted on X.

But it was El-Sayed who first made Piker central to his campaign by bringing him out on the trail, partying poolside with him at an influencer event, and celebrating with him during his Election Night rally. In his thousands of hours of streaming, Piker has produced a dense catalog of comments spanning the spectrum from stupid to incredibly offensive, including several iterations of the phrase “I hate America” and, perhaps most memorably, that “America deserved 9/11.” (He quickly attempted to walk it back.) Piker also flaunts his authoritarian sympathies, calling Mao Zedong “one of the great leaders of this world” and counting the collapse of the Soviet Union among the “catastrophes” of the 20th century. Last week, he warned that “eventually someone is going to come around and take action” against American Jews who are “singularly invested in Israel.”

Hasan Piker is part of the conversation now. He has become central to the Republican strategy in Michigan, where El-Sayed will continue to be asked about him. So, too, will Democrats across the country. The question ahead of November is whether their answers will satisfy voters.

El-Sayed has moved away from Piker since winning the primary last month. The streamer has not been on the trail in Michigan. “I have spoken with the good doctor,” Representative Jim Clyburn told reporters of El-Sayed, who has a medical degree. “He has apologized. He says he will not campaign with Piker anymore.” After Piker’s comments last week about American Jews, El-Sayed said in a statement that anti-Semitism is a “scourge” and that “I stand against any rhetoric that puts the community at risk.” When asked about Piker at a meeting with a group of Jewish Democrats on Saturday, though, El-Sayed declined to disavow him. “If you want to make this race about a streamer in California, I just think you’re missing the boat.”

Anyone could have predicted the Piker blowback. Plenty of people did. In March, one of El-Sayed’s primary opponents, Mallory McMorrow, compared Piker to the white-supremacist influencer Nick Fuentes, and leaders of the centrist think tank Third Way wrote a column urging Democrats not to associate with Piker. “Everyone saw it coming from a mile away, so they should’ve been better prepared to handle it,” one Democratic strategist told me. Even some of El-Sayed’s own backers felt similarly. “Not all socialism is toxic to the Democratic brand, but Piker certainly is,” one progressive strategist told me.

(None of the Democrat-aligned operatives I reached out to would agree to speak on the record for this story, citing their support for El-Sayed as well as their fear of reprisal from Piker’s rabid online fans.)

The Piker drama is a ribbon-wrapped gift to Republicans in a year when so much else—inflation, high gas prices, an unpopular president—is working against them. They seem well aware of this. Mike Rogers, El-Sayed’s Republican opponent, refers to Piker as El-Sayed’s “running mate.” “When I see Abdul El-Sayed campaign around this state with somebody who said that America deserved 9/11, what I see is a man who has sympathy and compassion for people who share his religion, but has nothing for people who don’t,” Vance said at the rally on Monday. “What I’d ask you to remember is that whoever you send to Washington, whatever policy views you have or you don’t have, send people of good heart who focus on the right issues, who fight for the right people, and who love the United States of America.” The strategy is obvious: Identify every repellent thing Piker has ever said, tie Piker to El-Sayed, and advertise the relationship at every opportunity.

There is more than a hint of irony in this situation. President Trump has shown a strong affinity for shock jocks and trolls. In 2020, he awarded Rush Limbaugh, who had a recurring segment celebrating the deaths of gay people from AIDS, the Presidential Medal of Freedom. Laura Loomer, a far-right activist and an ally of Trump’s, last week referred to a Senate candidate as a “ghetto black communist bitch.” Some Democrats, seeing Trump suffer little political consequence for such associations, believe it’s unfair that El-Sayed should have to answer for Piker’s actions.

But politics, like life, is famously unfair. Democrats are constantly being asked to condemn Piker in cable-news hits and hallway interviews, even outside Michigan. Several Jewish Democrats have weighed in too. Through a spokesperson, Ossoff said he “unreservedly rejects reckless and dangerous rhetoric suggesting that policy advocacy invites violence against the Jewish community or any community.” Representative Josh Gottheimer of New Jersey said that “anyone who campaigns with Piker or elevates him is complicit in the rising antisemitism and anti-American hatred in this country.” Moderate Democrats are seizing the moment as a chance to engage in a little centrist posturing. Senator John Fetterman went on Fox News and delivered a challenge to El-Sayed: “I’m offering $50,000 for you to do a rally with Hasan Piker” on September 11, he said. Piker was not immediately available for comment for this story. But last week, after several Jewish Democrats criticized him, he dismissed their concerns by implying they reflected an orchestrated conspiracy against him, writing on X that an “aipac boss call was made.”

Maybe El-Sayed could quell some of the frenzy himself. In 2008, controversial comments from Barack Obama’s former pastor Jeremiah Wright threatened to upend Obama’s bid for the White House. In a sermon shortly after September 11, the pastor said that “America’s chickens are coming home to roost.” Later, Wright said, “No, no, no, not God Bless America. God damn America—that’s in the Bible—for killing innocent people.”

Obama chose to address the controversy directly, and delivered a speech condemning Wright’s remarks while offering context about America’s racial tensions. That speech “was a masterpiece of empathy, and at the time it felt that it changed the trajectory of his campaign,” Michelle Goldberg wrote this week. At the very least, some Democrats argue, El-Sayed could more plainly denounce his friend. “Say, ‘Here’s what I condemn; here’s what I disavow. I disagree; it was wrong and hurtful,’” the progressive strategist said. “If Piker says something new that’s bad—which, if I was a betting man, I’d say will happen—you come out against it swiftly.”

Michigan, a state that Trump won in 2016 and 2024, was never going to be an easy win for El-Sayed. His relationship with Piker, who is paid to provoke, not persuade, isn’t going to make that task any simpler. The good news for Democrats is that most people don’t actually know Piker; polling from earlier this year showed that 60 percent of likely voters have never heard of him. The bad news for Democrats is that Republicans will spend the next two months working diligently to change that.

entries.title: An Alien Scholar’s Notes on Trump’s Washington
entries.summary: Why did he hate one pool so much?
entries.content:
We’ll start this conference looking back on 2026 Washington Architecture by being honest: We have no idea what happened here. The snapshot of this planet that my comrades and I managed to obtain on our brief visit left us, if anything, more confused about Earth than we had been before. What follows are theories only.

All we know of 21st-century human political figure Donald J. Trump is what we can guess from the architectural record and a few bits of digital evidence. (Due to a misunderstanding, we ate most of the written records of this planet before figuring out that they contained information.) Was he a builder or a destroyer? There are also ruins of an arch—commemorating a triumph, but over what? Perhaps the successful defeat of 250 years of democracy, a system of rule that he despised?

Did he have access to the internet (a human technology that seems to have been primarily used for the sharing of pornography and misinformation)? Impossible to say. Some records suggest that a female of his species accessed the internet on his behalf. We don’t know his exact relation to this female, but we can observe that she was swift of foot and skilled at concealment in small enclosures, probably a trait admired by others. Were such relationships common? Did many human leaders consider it an honor to be chased by another human carrying a printer? (Did George Washington have a “Human Printer” of his own? Perhaps Benjamin Franklin fulfilled this role?)

Although other human figures enjoyed construction, Trump seemed to prefer the wrecking ball (what we would refer to as Grogon’s Tail) as a mode of expression. From a forensic analysis of these structures, we know that the Smashing of the Residence was first to take place, followed by the Desecration of the Pool.

Donald Trump seems to have smashed the Residence deliberately, as a warning to rivals. As his nestlings were at that time all mature and dwelling independently, such a gesture posed no danger to his young. Some papers we found suggested that there were plans to put something in the enormous hole, but these drawings are on an unlikely scale, and their suggested purpose is inconsistent. Ballroom? Bunker? No one can seem to agree, not even the plans themselves.

The situation of the pool is puzzling. We may never know why Donald Trump hated the pool (pond?) so much, but his action to strip it of its water, paint over its interior with a humiliating sealant, and fill it with a thick green algae speaks of immense disrespect. Had the pool or pond offended him? We know from the many banners he left bearing his visage around the city that he seems to have been incapable of smiling; a golden idol located in Florida represents him as having a slightly melted appearance. Perhaps glimpsing his reflection in the pond reminded him unpleasantly of these facts? Or were its ducks hostile to him? Some records show that even when the pool was drained of water, it was patrolled by an armed guard; what danger lurked in its shallows?

The structure with the giant head in it puzzles us most. We think this site on the Potomac may once have been used for entertainment and functioned as a kind of temple to the performing arts. Others suggest that it was an oversize dwelling place for mice. Some scholars believe that people really went inside the building and sat in red chairs while someone stood and bellowed in Italian. Perhaps this hall was used for punishment? Were wrongdoers subjected to the “tuba”?

Letters found near the site marking it “The Donald J. Trump and the John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts” suggest that the enormous bronze head may represent either Donald J. Trump or John F. Kennedy, in whose joint memory the center seems to have been erected. Who were these men? They must have loved the arts. Perhaps an American Harmodius and Aristogeiton? Curiously, we do not see them commemorated jointly in other locations.

Some scholars argue that Donald J. Trump was in fact alive at the time of the center’s commemoration, but other scholars reply that this claim is ludicrous—where else is there evidence of a Memorial Center constructed while its subject was still living? The same theory suggests that he added his name to the center decades after its construction, halted all the shows, removed the public artworks, and threatened to demolish it if his name was not kept on, but other scholars reply that smashing things unless you can write your name on them is hardly the behavior of a full-fledged adult. We truly don’t know what to make of this place. (Just for the record, though, we didn’t do the pyramids.)

entries.title: The Sexual Politics of the ‘Bed Trick’
entries.summary: A new book about an infamous trial asks how the stories we tell can define our relationships.
entries.content:
A new book about an infamous trial asks how the stories we tell can define our relationships.

A decade ago in northern England, a young woman named Gayle Newland was convicted—twice—of an unusual crime. Another woman, who was known variously as “Chloe” and “Miss X” in court documents and media reports, reported that she’d been a victim of sexual fraud. Newland, she said, had posed as a chronically ill man named Kye Fortune in order to become her lover; the gender deception was enabled by the use of a blindfold during sex. But whenever Newland took the witness stand to testify, she shared an entirely different version of events. She and Miss X were best friends and closeted lesbians, she said, and Kye was their shared fantasy, sustained over several years.

According to the British newspapers, particularly tabloids such as The Daily Mail and the Daily Express, the story was simple: Newland was a predator, carefully tricking her heterosexual friend into a lesbian relationship by pretending to be a man. The legal system and the juries affirmed this reporting, finding Newland guilty twice (the original conviction was overturned on a technicality). Newland’s actions resembled the kind of madcap fiction in which someone pretends to be the opposite sex and hijinks ensue (as in Twelfth Night or The Rocky Horror Picture Show); pretends to be someone’s husband in the dark (as in Chaucer’s The Canterbury Tales); or changes sex outright, raising deeper questions (as in Virginia Woolf’s Orlando).

But Izabella Scott, whose new book, The Bed Trick, is an astoundingly well-calibrated mixture of legal reporting and literary analysis, knows full well that a heavily publicized trial is hardly the best venue for understanding other people—especially how other people have sex. “Trials are storytelling contests,” Scott writes. “They are making a case, producing stories—competitive stories that use extremes in order to win.”

Scott is rightfully less interested in figuring out whether the verdict was correct (because it’s been litigated already) than in what the case illuminates about gender and truth. What preoccupies her is how the narrative device of the “bed trick,” so common in fiction and so rare in real life, came to fruition as a contest of wills between two young women. She wants to understand how two wildly disparate stories were created, what those stories tell us about ourselves, and what continues to make many people so anxious about relationships and behaviors that defy traditional norms.

The Newland trials are rich texts, and Scott pores over every transcript page, looking for meaning. The case, one of sexual assault with elements of fraud, was developed in line with the U.K.’s most recent Sexual Offences Act, which was passed in 2003 and nullified consent in situations where “the defendant intentionally deceived the complainant as to the nature or purpose of the relevant act.” Scott defines this version of rape as “a violation of sexual autonomy—that is, a violation of personal freedom, of choice, and thus a violation of selfhood, identity, perhaps even humanity.”

Rape cases are notoriously difficult to prosecute; only a sliver of those reported (themselves a likely undercount of incidents) go to trial, and few result in a conviction. The Newland case was even more unusual, because the first conviction hinged on Section 76 of the Sexual Offences Act—the clause about deceit. (The second conviction drew on a different case, R v. McNally, which ruled that “deception as to gender can vitiate consent.”) What Miss X alleged was more complex than a simple violation of “no means no”: Because Miss X had been deceived, her yeses were built on a lie.

This deception was multilayered, as Scott discovers and analyzes. Miss X came from a religious background, was estranged from her parents, and had reportedly ended an abusive relationship recently, making her especially vulnerable—whether as a closeted queer woman, as Newland attested, or as, according to Miss X, a straight woman in love with a chronically ill man whose face and body she never saw during sex. Newland first concocted the “Kye Fortune” character online at the age of 13, swiping pictures and videos from a half-Asian man named Carlo over several years. Other women reported having been duped by “Kye” online before discovering that their correspondent wasn’t a man. And after the 2017 conviction, jurors learned that Newland had also been convicted of financial fraud.

But Newland stuck to her story, claiming that she and Miss X met at a gay bar, came out to each other, and shared in the “Kye” fantasy together, although they still felt compelled to stay in the closet. (The evidence for this narrative is not strong.) Newland grew up with loving parents, owned a car, and had an allowance, but she claimed that at the all-girls private school she attended, the word lesbian was a slur, conditioning her to feel lasting shame about her sexuality. She sobbed repeatedly while on the stand, even as her story wavered in its details.

Scott is merciful toward Newland, affording her the benefit of the doubt that the media, and especially the legal system, couldn’t or wouldn’t. The legal acceptance of queer relationships is still a recent development, and delineating the ways in which queer sex can work—with objects and implements, with kink and other proclivities not traditionally associated with heterosexual relationships—seemed to baffle the barristers during direct questioning and cross-examination.

For Scott, reading through the transcripts became an exercise in the absurd, more like Nikolai Gogol’s “The Nose” than a typical true-crime tale. How could it not, with almost every controversial issue—race, class, queerness, gender, disability rights, consent—under the bright lights? “To read their stories is to find both” Newland and Miss X “entering a topsy-turvy world,” Scott writes, “their reason clouded by fantasy and hope, blinkered and madly doting. Both stepped over some line and their reason evaporated.”

The loss of reason wasn’t exclusive to these young women, once so intimate and now such bitter adversaries. The Newland trials foreshadowed later debates about gender fluidity and sexuality, culminating in the 2025 U.K. Supreme Court ruling that the legal term woman refers to a biological woman. The Newland case featured an extreme manifestation of Britain’s cultural discomfort with shifting gender norms, but in the years since, that unease has led to decisions that are damaging the lives of many people who simply want to be left alone to be themselves.

In spite of Scott’s rigorous forensic examination of the case, it is impossible to know with certainty what happened between Newland and Miss X. Their stories diverged markedly, but that divergence remained largely consistent across the trials: two irreconcilable versions of one relationship. Scott suggests that Newland and Miss X found the plots they needed to make themselves whole, as individuals and as a couple—whether they were best friends or closeted lesbian lovers.

Scott knows that she, too, is telling a story. “In my attempt to know, I construct a plot,” she writes. “In a way, this book is a shadow trial.” She writes that she is “using literary tools, like suspense and points of view,” and implores readers never to forget this. In the process, she puts storytelling itself on trial: “I think about the stories that grip us in life, but also in court. I wonder why some stories are more believable than others.”

Wisely, she doesn’t offer a grand unified theory of what happened between Miss X and Newland. She cannot. She knows the limits of narrative too well to do so. Still, the crime reporter in me latched on to a particular narrative contradiction, one that might point to the inciting incident that pulled the thread of deception and unraveled what was supposed to be the shared story.

Newland and Miss X agree that it all fell apart one night. In Miss X’s version, “something just felt different.” Newland had insisted on oral sex; Miss X was reluctant, and the act was rough. Shortly afterward, she testified, she took her blindfold off and realized “Kye” was a woman—and had been using a prosthesis. In Newland’s version, their fight that evening resulted from Newland’s decision to come out as gay—a violation of their “pact.” Although Newland denied having oral sex, I wondered why Scott doesn’t spend more time exploring a third narrative: that this was a moment of muddled consent in a complicated situation. It seems plausible to me that Newland went ahead with a sexual act her partner simply didn’t want. And in the aftermath, she might have realized that the game had gone too far, and that the trust she’d been so careful to build was broken forever.

When she began working on The Bed Trick, Scott thought it would be primarily an exploration of rape law, but by the end, she realized it had more to do with the relationship between the law and fiction. In the process, she also dug up her own buried memories of a long-ago assault in a different country, an incident that proved to be so emotionally painful, and the bureaucracy involved in pursuing the case so burdensome, that she ended up dropping it. But the connections between her experience and the Newland case aren’t simple, just as the trial she writes about occupies all manner of messy borders. “There is no final answer,” she writes, “to what is deception and what is true.”

Newland ultimately served a total of six years in prison. In 2024, a fashion influencer took to TikTok to recount her own astounding story: Her girlfriend, whom she’d featured in at least one video, had been revealed by various commenters to be Newland. The influencer ended the relationship. Newland, it seems, won’t be allowed to move on from her past. Miss X, at least, has the cloak of privacy to protect her.

entries.title: Gloria Steinem’s Feminism for All
entries.summary: The activist and writer, who died yesterday at the age of 92, steadfastly fought for her belief that women could change the world together.
entries.content:
The activist and writer, who died yesterday at the age of 92, steadfastly fought for her belief that women could change the world together.

This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter. Sign up for it here.

Throughout most of Gloria Steinem’s life, two versions of her existed. Publicly, Steinem was a figurehead: the glamorous co-founder of Ms. magazine, a totem for second-wave feminism and a bull’s-eye for its detractors, gorgeously inscrutable behind her curtains of streaked hair and tinted glasses. Privately, she was a workhorse: someone who hid behind her accessories, felt she’d come to the women’s movement late (in her mid-30s), and spent much of the rest of her life hustling to make up for it. If these two identities came into conflict—the persona and the person, the superstar feminist who was terrified of public speaking—Steinem, who died yesterday at the age of 92, simply pushed on. Her politics and her life both revolved around her steadfast commitment to the idea that all women are human beings deserving of equal opportunity, and that uniting around this concept could change the world.

Steinem has said she was radicalized in 1969, around her 35th birthday, when, as one of the founding journalists working for Clay Felker’s New York magazine, she covered an abortion-rights “speak-out” in Greenwich Village, where she learned that as many as one in three American women had terminated a pregnancy. The statistic shocked her, if not the procedure—a little more than a decade earlier, when Steinem was 22 and a recent Smith College graduate, she’d had one herself. Years later, the way she’d been led to cordon it off as a private incident got stuck in her brain. It was, she later wrote in her 2015 memoir, My Life on the Road, a “click of consciousness—namely, that I had been silent and silenced.” (She dedicated that book to the London doctor who had performed her abortion.) She realized that, like so many other women, she’d “been made to feel at fault, not realizing there were political reasons why female humans were not supposed to make decisions about our own bodies.” For New York, Steinem wrote a report titled “After Black Power, Women’s Liberation,” one of the first major dispatches on a national movement that was starting to take form.

In her article, Steinem set out her thesis that for the women’s movement to be effective, it would have to be inclusive, bringing together different factions and activist groups. Throughout the 1960s, feminism had manifested most publicly as an expression of discontent among middle-class white women in the suburbs, while Black feminists worked on the fringes of the civil-rights movement and domestic workers struggled to be recognized by labor organizers. In 1963, Betty Friedan published The Feminine Mystique, a book that exposed the pervasive unhappiness of so many overeducated, underemployed housewives. By 1969, it had become clearer to many activists that forming alliances on behalf of all women might, as Steinem wrote, “forge the final revolutionary link.”

Feminists were rallying around the idea that the personal is political, something Steinem knew intimately. Her mother, Ruth, had been a reporter and an editor for a newspaper in Toledo, Ohio, and her paternal grandmother had been one of the first Jewish women elected to public office in the United States. Before Steinem was born, her mother had had a nervous breakdown, and she became addicted to the chloral hydrate prescribed to her by a doctor. Her father, a traveling antiques salesman, took the family on the road for much of every year. When Steinem was roughly 10, her parents separated, and she was left to care for Ruth alone, bringing her toast and coffee while her mother lay in bed “with eyes closed and lips moving in occasional response to voices only she could hear,” as Steinem would later describe it. Steinem didn’t blame her mother for an intensely difficult childhood, seeing Ruth’s life as proof of how unequally women were suffering.

“The middle-class, educated and disillusioned group gets larger with each college graduation,” Steinem wrote in 1969. But she saw, too, that women for whom work was a need, not an opportunity, were equally deserving of representation. When she was asked to speak publicly about women’s liberation after her New York report was published, she decided to take a friend, Dorothy Pitman Hughes, with her. “Right away we discovered that a white woman and a black woman speaking together attracted far more diverse audiences than either one of us would have done on our own,” she wrote in her memoir. She formed lifelong partnerships and friendships with some of the 20th century’s most influential activists—Florynce Kennedy, Wilma Mankiller, bell hooks—and was the treasurer for the legal fund for the defense of Angela Davis.

At the end of 1971, Steinem, with a collective of writers and editors, launched Ms., a magazine that debuted as a 40-page insert tucked inside New York. The idea for a feminist publication came about during meetings when people in the movement lamented that they couldn’t get meaningful stories about women published. Steinem suggested a newsletter. Brenda Feigen, who’d co-founded the Women’s Action Alliance with her, countered with the idea of a glossy magazine, a product that seemed familiar enough to appeal to women who weren’t already aligned with the cause. Even from the beginning, there were fractures between those who saw the insurgent potential of a mainstream feminist magazine and those who wanted something more radical. “We came out against marriage and motherhood,” the feminist writer Vivian Gornick said of the latter faction, in a 2011 oral history of Ms. “Gloria was uptown; we were downtown. She hung out with Establishment figures; we had only ourselves.” (Steinem pushed back later by saying that the only reason she lived uptown was that she couldn’t afford a place in the Village. She herself never had children and joked that she married in 2000, at the age of 66, only to help secure the immigration status of her husband, the entrepreneur and activist David Bale; Bale died of cancer three years later.)

The first full issue of Ms., published in January 1972, featured an image reimagining the Hindu goddess Kali as a housewife, each of her eight arms clutching a different household item while tears stream down her face. Inside the magazine were articles on sisterhood among feminists and raising children without adhering to traditional gender roles, as well as a groundbreaking statement signed by 53 women—Steinem, Anaïs Nin, and Billie Jean King among them—noting that they had had abortions. All 300,000 printed copies sold out in eight days. Mailbags jammed with letters began arriving at the office. The magazine was broadly mocked in mainstream publications, on TV news, and even in the White House: President Richard Nixon was caught on tape deriding Steinem to Henry Kissinger.

Anyone co-opted as a figurehead becomes vulnerable to charges of grandiosity, but the vitriol directed at Steinem for much of the ’70s and ’80s was almost unprecedented. In 1963, while trying to establish herself as a freelance writer, she’d worked undercover at Playboy’s Bunny Club in Manhattan, detailing how women were subjected to internal gynecological examinations, and were routinely groped and otherwise harassed under horrific working conditions. The report caused a stir, but it also cast Steinem in many people’s minds as a lightweight who used her looks to get ahead. Because Ms. often struggled to sell ads, Steinem was obliged to fundraise for donations to keep the magazine going, appearing in public as a spokesperson for feminism in a way that galled other women in the movement. Steinem’s sphinxlike distance—she hid behind her hair, she said, because she’d always been sensitive about the roundness of her face—also fueled her detractors. “Gloria has all the irritating qualities of a saint,” Liz Smith wrote in 1971, according to Vanity Fair. By 1975, radical feminists publicly had distanced themselves from Ms., whose politics the writer Ellen Willis described as “a mushy, sentimental idea of sisterhood designed to obscure political conflicts between women.”

In her memoir, Steinem was sanguine about experiencing decades of what a Ms. article described as “trashing,” or “the dark side of sisterhood.” Needing approval, she wrote, “is a female cultural disease, and often a sign of doing the wrong thing.” What often gets obscured in any discussion of feminist infighting is the scale of what the women’s-liberation movement managed to achieve during the 1970s: landmark legal victories regarding reproductive rights, sex discrimination in the workplace, and access to education; the establishment of dozens of shelters across the country for women who were victims of domestic abuse; the passage of the Equal Rights Amendment, although it was never ratified.

For Steinem, the most significant moment in her life was the 1977 National Women’s Conference in Houston, an event Steinem later described as “the most important event nobody knows about.” In 1971, she’d worked with three female representatives, Bella Abzug, Shirley Chisholm, and Patsy Mink, to establish the National Political Women’s Caucus. Now Abzug was drafting all three women to help support the unimaginable: an official platform for women in America, voted on by delegates for diverse groups from all over the country. Steinem was asked to be a “token” by groups from the so-called Minority Women’s Plank, to record their concerns and conflicts and draft language that could be combined into a single text. “Before Houston, I had known that women in small groups could be courageous and loyal to each other and respect each other’s differences,” Steinem recalled in her memoir. “After Houston, I’d learned that women could do this in large numbers, across chasms of difference, and for serious purpose.” She was prouder of her role at the conference than of anything else she’d ever done.

For the rest of her life, and the rest of her career as an activist and a writer, she maintained this belief in what women are capable of when they can find common ground. “We are linked,” she once said, “not ranked.” She felt that true feminism would ultimately liberate everyone, not least men. And she was adamant that in-person meetings, in which people could gather to listen to one another, were crucial for bringing about change and fostering community. She continued to host “talking circles” at her home into her 90s, discussing reproductive health, inclusivity, and AI over the past year, and she placed her apartment in a trust so that others can continue her work there in the years to come. She saw herself fundamentally as an activist, not a theorist, and believed that the diversity of the women’s movement was also its strength. “I think I’ve wasted some of my time, but used most of it well, and have realized that my life is not separate from other people’s lives or from the universe,” Steinem told Interview in 2011. “I think our moments of happiness really come from a feeling of unity.”

entries.title: The Schism Within the Trump Administration on Mexico
entries.summary: Officials are veering between praise for cooperation and threats to attack.
entries.content:
Officials are veering between praise for cooperation and threats to attack.

To hear Ronald D. Johnson tell it, the United States and Mexico have entered an era of blissful cooperation. Johnson, a former Army and intelligence officer who took up his post as U.S. ambassador to Mexico in the spring of 2025, has chronicled on his social-media feeds joint efforts to incapacitate drug cartels, tackle the screwworm pandemic, halt illegal immigration, imprison wildlife traffickers, dismantle criminal finance networks, and expand soybean exports. That’s just over the past two weeks.

For Johnson, the U.S.–Mexico relationship is defined by “close coordination,” “decisive action,” “information shared,” and “the security of both our nations.” His hashtag of choice is #TogetherWeAchieveMore. Johnson’s Mexico is one in which the country’s security chief, nicknamed Batman, has made remarkable strides against criminal networks.

Other members of the Trump administration see things differently. Stephen Miller’s Mexico has a cartel-dominated government that has obstinately refused to cooperate in the fight against drugs and illegal immigration. It’s a place where terrorist organizations “kill, extort, kidnap, or murder anybody who gets in their way,” as he said in a July speech. Miller’s Mexico is one in which the U.S. military might need to do what an ineffectual Mexican government cannot.

Perhaps no other bilateral relationship has exposed so publicly the stark disconnects within the Trump administration. Mexican officials say they have become accustomed to bipolarity—a “doble discurso,” they call it—in their interactions with the U.S. government. Some meetings suggest that things are going swimmingly. Others seem to telegraph the possibility of an American air strike. “Sometimes they say one thing, and other times they say another” was how Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum explained the vacillation during a press conference in August.

Last week, after Johnson’s run of public praise, U.S. officials revived a periodic critique against Mexico in meetings in Washington between Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the Mexican foreign minister, Roberto Velasco: Mexico isn’t doing enough to stop its own citizens from migrating to the United States. More than half of the people apprehended by U.S. Border Patrol in July were Mexican. U.S. officials asked why Mexico couldn’t halt the flow of its own citizens.

To Mexican officials, it felt like an unfair demand, given how much they had already offered the U.S. on immigration enforcement. Although overall apprehensions at the U.S.-Mexico border are up slightly from last year, they are down roughly 90 percent from 2023, thanks in part to Mexican cooperation. And although Mexican authorities have made it much more difficult for migrants from other countries to approach the border, deterring Mexicans presents a different sort of challenge. Detaining Mexicans moving through their own country “would be a violation of Mexican law,” the country’s former immigration chief Tonatiuh Guillén López told us. “It would pin the state against its own citizens.”

Johnson had posted on X that the Rubio meeting “reflects our commitment to work together to stop illegal migration.” But the secretary’s office struck a different tone, suggesting that Rubio wasn’t satisfied with what he had heard. Rubio, a post-meeting readout from the department explained, had “called for decisive action to end illegal immigration, stop the trafficking of fentanyl and other illicit drugs into the United States, and dismantle foreign terrorist organizations and cartels and deprive them of arms.”

Asked about the inconsistency in messaging about Mexico, the White House echoed Miller’s sentiments. “As President Trump has said, and as the U.S. government has repeatedly and clearly communicated, it is unacceptable that foreign terrorist organizations control vast territories across Mexico, including the entire region that directly borders the United States,” the White House spokesperson Lauren Bis told us in a statement.

The United States’ most important trade agreement could get caught in the tug-of-war over whether Mexico is doing enough to further U.S. interests. As the United States, Mexico, and Canada work through the annual review of the trilateral USMCA trade deal, Miller has privately floated the possibility that the U.S. could use the occasion to pressure Mexico into doing more on immigration enforcement, one U.S. official said. Although the focus of the USMCA review has been more on granular disputes over supply chains and the origins of raw materials, the U.S. could decide to withdraw from the deal entirely. If that happened, the economic blow to all three countries would be substantial.

U.S. law-enforcement officials based in Mexico gush about the kind of close security coordination that they’re seeing now, but that hadn’t existed for more than a decade. Since Sheinbaum’s election in 2024, Mexico has acted on U.S. intelligence to take down top cartel leaders; it has extradited more than 100 alleged criminals to the United States; it has detained thousands of migrants en route to the U.S. border and permitted thousands of non-Mexican deportees from the U.S. to be sent to southern Mexico. Sheinbaum’s predecessor openly considered stripping Drug Enforcement Administration agents of diplomatic immunity; now those agents have supported a series of major security operations.

“On security cooperation, what we’ve seen is a massive improvement under Sheinbaum. We’re getting things that were blocked for years—from extraditions to action against cartels,” one recently retired U.S. official who had been based in Mexico told us.

But for another group of U.S. officials, those actions are grossly insufficient. Miller in particular has lobbied for unilateral U.S. action against Mexican cartels. When he meets with Mexican officials, he typically complains about the country’s inaction. During Fox News interviews, he has used Mexico City, along with Baghdad, as examples of the world’s most dangerous cities. Sheinbaum has responded by saying she asked her foreign minister to send “this White House official the data concerning Mexico City, which perhaps he is not aware of.” (Mexico City has roughly the same homicide rate as Portland, Oregon.)

In recent weeks, U.S. diplomatic and trade officials have grown worried that the USMCA, negotiated during Trump’s first term, could be blown up if some of the president’s advisers get their way. U.S.-Canada relations are already strained over bilateral disputes; now negotiators fear that the broader pact could become a casualty of Trump’s immigration and cartel crackdowns.

Peter Navarro, a senior adviser to Trump on trade and manufacturing, has cast doubt on the deal, arguing that it needs major changes or should be scrapped altogether. Mexico is the United States’ largest trading partner—another point that Johnson makes frequently, but something that Navarro and other members of the Trump administration seem to view as a liability.

The deal enables a regional supply chain in which parts of a final product are sourced and assembled across the three countries. If the USMCA were to be abandoned or weakened, manufacturing costs throughout North America would rise dramatically. But the stakes of any USMCA renegotiation go well beyond the future of a trade pact. If the administration uses the deal to gain leverage over immigration and security policy, it would blur the line between trade policy and national security, and put the basic rules governing North American commerce at the mercy of disputes far outside trade. For Mexico, that could make the USMCA review less a negotiation over tariff rates than a test of how far the government is willing to bend to Washington’s demands. Mexico is already watching the U.S.-Canada rupture closely as it prepares for its own talks with Washington.

Trump allies have long touted his unpredictability as an asset, and Mexican journalists and security analysts are now debating whether the incoherence within the administration is perhaps part of a broader strategy. “Ambiguity is the tool. As long as Mexico doesn’t know for sure what will trigger the Pentagon and what will satisfy the DEA, it continues to hand over information,” Ghaleb Krame, an analyst and a former Mexican official, wrote in an August Substack post.

Other Mexican intellectuals argue that it’s Sheinbaum—the leader of a populist, leftist political party—who has revealed her own doble discurso in her dealings with the Americans. She “employs an anti-imperialist discourse for domestic consumption, while being discreetly and selectively subservient to the United States,” Ricardo Pascoe Pierce, a former Mexican congressman and ambassador, wrote in the newspaper El Heraldo de México. Sheinbaum has been particularly critical of the treatment of Mexican immigrants by U.S. immigration authorities, asking U.S. state attorneys general to investigate the deaths of 17 Mexican nationals in ICE detention or enforcement operations. But that anger has apparently not affected Mexico’s cooperation with the U.S. on security or immigration enforcement.

Johnson was the first U.S. ambassador in Trump’s second term to have an official Truth Social account. There and on X, he is careful to tag the president in his posts, signaling Mexico’s progress and growing cooperation. Johnson, who declined an interview request, has good reason to make sure the White House is aware of his messaging: Trump himself has embodied the kind of duality in his remarks about Mexico that ripples across his administration. He has called Sheinbaum “terrific” and “elegant,” with “a beautiful voice.” He has also said, repeatedly, that “the cartels rule Mexico.”

Johnson’s efforts to convey to Trump the payoff from Mexican cooperation may be working. Even though Miller has promoted a unilateral strike on Mexico—presumably targeting a cartel hideout or fentanyl lab—no such attack has occurred. U.S. officials in Mexico know that unilateral action would have an immediate chilling effect on bilateral cooperation, and they hope that it can be deterred. They have privately told their Mexican counterparts that anticartel efforts will be coordinated jointly.

Even some of the U.S. officials most critical of Mexico seem to recognize the value of the country’s assistance. DEA Administrator Terry Cole in July called the Mexican government and cartels “one and the same.” But a month later, at a presentation in Argentina, he told a story about Mexico’s security chief, Omar García Harfuch, calling to inform the Americans that Mexican security forces had killed Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes, known as El Mencho, arguably the most dangerous drug trafficker in the region. Cole sat next to Harfuch as he recounted the story and described the joint celebration after El Mencho’s death. “Omar and I share information daily,” he said.

It was another disorienting twist for those following U.S.-Mexico relations, trying to parse what exactly the Trump administration makes of its southern neighbor. Former U.S. officials told us that part of the apparent inconsistency in White House messaging is related to Mexico’s own internal contradictions: a country with a $2 trillion licit economy where organized crime controls large swaths of territory; a government that attacks cartels even as some of its own members are accused of aiding organized crime. The U.S. government has always had difficulty capturing that nuance in its messaging. Now it doesn’t even seem to be trying.

entries.title: The Netherlands Will Never Be Rid of Louisiana Crawfish
entries.summary: What will it take for the Dutch to eat them?
entries.content:
What will it take for the Dutch to eat them?

Confronted with a seasoned, boiled, arguably delicious crayfish, some of the people of the Netherlands are not sure exactly what to do. “Do you suck the head out?” I heard from the table next to me earlier this summer, at Two Chefs, a restaurant in Amsterdam that hosts a monthly crayfish boil.



Yes is the answer: The best way to eat a crayfish is to shell the tail, then slurp the flavored juices out of the head, and pick out the remaining meat with your hands.

This strategy might not be an immediate transatlantic hit. At the boil, one 29-year-old from Maastricht likened the meal to shrimp but with more work. Two twins told me that the crayfish would need to look a little more chic on the plate to appeal to the Dutch public. But, given the ever-growing population of crayfish in the Netherlands, coming around to eating more of them could benefit the country.

Because if Dutch consumers aren’t sure how they feel about crayfish, crayfish inarguably love the Netherlands. They have invaded the country’s waterways so thoroughly that they have become a real problem, and dealing with them will mean persuading more creatures—including Dutch people—to eat more crayfish.

The crayfish invasion started decades ago, but in recent years, the red swamp crayfish (also known as the Louisiana crawfish) has become a particular pest, Pim Lemmers, an ecologist at Radboud University who has dedicated his career to researching crayfish, told me. In the 1980s, it was brought to the Netherlands as food, and people naively released the animals into the environment. The waterways in the Netherlands are very interconnected and became a “crayfish highway” of sorts, Ivo Roessink, an aquatic ecotoxicologist at Wageningen University & Research, told me. But crayfish can walk and breathe on land, too, and have been spotted in parks, along bike lanes, and at Schiphol airport, where the birds use the runway to crush them.

And they can dig—burrows up to three feet long that can collapse the edges of fields into the water and that some people fear could damage the country’s extensive system of dams, dikes, and canals. Scientists emphasize that the risk to dams and dikes is low; from their point of view, the bigger risk is to other creatures that live in the water. Crayfish are omnivorous: “They totally destroy underwater vegetation,” Roessink said. They also eat detritus, amphibian and insect larvae, snails and other invertebrates, small fish, and one another—a sight I witnessed for myself.

But crayfish cannibalism will not end the invasion; in fact, although the Netherlands’ central government is working on a program for crayfish management, getting rid of the species will likely be impossible. “I know of one example where they effectively eradicated crayfish, and that was in the U.S.,” Roessink said. “There was an infected pond, and they turned it into a parking lot.” (Resorting to this solution in the Netherlands would require paving over the entire country.) Research in the Netherlands and elsewhere has shown that even extensive trapping won’t necessarily eliminate crayfish. The most anyone can hope for is fewer of them.

Some water boards of the Netherlands are trying to persuade all sorts of creatures to eat more crayfish, including herons, eels, and European catfish, which are themselves something of an invasive threat. And, in theory, one of the crayfish’s most effective predators could be Dutch people.

Stefan van Ekris and Maarten van der Sanden, who are both managing directors at CrawFish Farm Holland, are trying their best to make it happen. This July, I joined them as they put on waders and immersed themselves in irrigation ditches to set and check their crayfish nets in the Groene Hart, or “Green Heart,” of the Netherlands, the thinly populated pastures and peatlands among some of the country’s largest cities. They get paid per kilogram caught—the expedition I joined yielded about 150 kilograms, or 330 pounds, of live crayfish—but this is really a passion project for them. CrawFish Farm Holland is approved to sell live and prepared catch directly to restaurants and other wholesalers, and hopes to sell its crayfish in supermarkets in the next two years. “We’re not cultivating them,” Van der Sanden told me. “We’re fighting them and eating them.”

In America, Van der Sanden pointed out, Louisiana was able to quickly ramp up crayfish production and demand in the 1980s. But the scientists I spoke with were skeptical of this strategy. “You will never eat yourself out of this crisis,” Roessink said. And if people like crayfish too much, Lemmers said, they might start cultivating crayfish in their backyard or trapping them without oversight, which could promote further spread. Even if more Dutch people come around to the pleasures of a messy boil, the crayfish still could come out ahead.

entries.title: What the Floods Say About Xi Jinping
entries.summary: China’s leader behaves more like an emperor than a man of the people.
entries.content:
China’s leader behaves more like an emperor than a man of the people.

When the Yangtze River flooded in 1998 and inundated villages in central China, Jiang Zemin, the Communist Party’s general secretary, was on the scene, bullhorn in hand, to encourage local relief efforts. Ten years later, his successor, Hu Jintao, stood among the rubble after an earthquake rocked Sichuan province, in the country’s southwest. Last week, after floodwaters caused by a collapsing glacier tore through the Himalayas between Nepal and China, leaving more than 1,100 people dead and thousands more missing, the party’s current general secretary, Xi Jinping, stayed largely and safely in Beijing.

In the United States, where politicians have to worry about the needs and feelings of voters, elected representatives are expected to be more visible and engaged in national crises. In 2021, Republican Senator Ted Cruz earned public condemnation when he was caught absconding to Mexico while Texas suffered a deep freeze and power outages. As a Communist dictator, Xi doesn’t have to fret over public-approval ratings. Yet his absence signals a bigger problem for China: Xi has become so powerful that he has lost touch with the country he governs.

Despite being professed Marxists, China’s leaders rarely interact with the working class. But Xi at least used to try to seem like a man of the people. In 2013, about a year into his tenure, Chinese media made a big deal out of his visit to a steamed-bun restaurant in Beijing; the state-owned China Daily praised him for showing his “common touch.”

Today, there’s nothing common about Xi Jinping. He has amassed greater personal power than any other Chinese leader since Mao Zedong, the Communist regime’s founder, who died half a century ago. To justify his outsize role in China’s government, Xi’s tireless propagandists portray him as something grander than a party boss: a philosopher king, whose doctrine of wisdom, called Xi Jinping Thought, is meant to be both studied and obeyed. He is the great global statesman, guiding foreign policy into a new era of peace and prosperity. His various “global initiatives” outline his vision for a reformed world order.

Mere mortals such as Jiang and Hu had to stomp around muddy disaster zones to prove their worth. But Xi “does not need to go to steam-bun shops to pretend he is with the people any longer, or, for that matter, to be visible when a major disaster has happened,” Steve Tsang, the director of the SOAS China Institute at the University of London, told me. “He no doubt thinks and therefore acts as if he is above all.”

In Xi’s calculus, the Himalayan communities destroyed by the floods are hardly worthy of his attention. The area in question is part of Tibet, a region that borders Nepal and was once independent. Xi has demonstrated a persistent hostility toward China’s minorities, who, in their stubborn resistance to Chinese civilization, threaten his vision of national unity. A new law that took effect in July aims to transform Tibetans, Uyghurs, Mongolians, and other minorities into properly loyal citizens by forcing them to adopt the majority Han Chinese culture. Until the Tibetans fall in line, “there is not really a compelling reason for him to visit them just because a disaster struck,” Tsang argued.

From Xi’s perspective, appearing at the scene of the floods would have involved more risk than reward. A purportedly all-knowing and all-seeing leader can’t make mistakes or even be associated with bad news, so Xi has good reason to avoid potentially tarnishing himself with an uncertain rescue operation. The politically safer option involves managing the crisis from afar while dispatching others to get their hands dirty. Beijing is also carefully controlling the information coming from the disaster zone. International journalists are already barred from Tibet, so any news about the disaster and the relief effort is from Chinese state sources. The state-run news agency Xinhua duly announced on Friday that Xi chaired a meeting of the party’s powerful Politburo to “deliberate and make arrangements on rescue and relief efforts.”

The China-focused research firm Trivium noted that Xi’s response to the floods was in keeping with his usual approach to disasters, which is to visit long after the crisis has passed and the rebuilding has begun. Xi is “keeping himself above operational risk” and is focused on “owning the recovery rather than the chaos,” Trivium’s report said. Xi may at some point decide to show up on the ground, but probably well after the initial chaos has subsided.

The stories and images from the floods have moved hearts, but Xi has bigger things to think about than a mudslide on the far edge of his empire. One of his priorities has been to reshape Chinese culture by merging the party’s beloved Marxism with traditional Confucianism. Although that effort appears to have had little traction with the public, Xi himself seems to have taken these ideas to heart. He may speak like a socialist, but he governs more like an emperor, deserving of national veneration and shielded from scrutiny. But many emperors were remote figures, removed from the real world behind the walls of the Forbidden City, and reliant on courtiers for news from outside. As Xi’s absence from the flooding disaster demonstrates, he, too, has become detached from the daily struggles and sentiments of his citizens—and unresponsive to the nation’s mounting economic and social problems as a result.

How the Chinese people feel about Xi’s response is impossible to know. Assiduous censors deter candor and cleanse social-media platforms of any direct criticism. Perhaps life in an authoritarian political system breeds a practical indifference, given that people have no influence over who rules them anyway. But with a spare few hours on the ground among those who just lost everything, Xi could have at least shown that he cares. His loyal public has surely noticed that even that was too much.

entries.title: Should We Be Afraid of Our Food?
entries.summary: America's food-safety system is being methodically dismantled by the Trump administration.
entries.content:
America's food-safety system is being methodically dismantled by the Trump administration.

The cyclosporiasis outbreak that has garnered so much attention in recent months is unquestionably bad news. People have been sickened in at least 48 states, and the number of lab-confirmed cases—about 17,000—represents only a fraction of the number of people who have been infected by the parasite.

But as foodborne illnesses go, a cyclospora infection—most likely caused in this instance by the consumption of iceberg lettuce contaminated with human feces—is relatively mild: unpleasant but rarely life-threatening. The two people who have died during the current outbreak had serious underlying conditions. Other foodborne pathogens are far more dangerous. More than 1 million Americans are sickened by Salmonella every year; invasive, potentially life-threatening infections occur in about 8 percent of lab-confirmed cases, and cause meningitis, sepsis, and other serious complications. A botulism infection can cause paralysis, seizures, nerve damage, lung damage, and brain damage, as well as death.

A few years ago, I reported here on an outbreak of Cronobacter infections linked to powdered infant formula and the subsequent recall by Abbott Nutrition. Two recent botulism outbreaks linked to powdered infant formula made by two other companies have thus far received little attention. During an outbreak that peaked in November 2025, at least 48 infants across 17 states were stricken with botulism traced to powdered formula from the company ByHeart. The infants were hospitalized with severe complications; one of them suffered multiple strokes. Then, earlier this year, at least four infants in three states were stricken with botulism from powdered formula made by the company Nara Organics. All four infants were hospitalized.

A key ingredient in the tainted formula sold by both companies was milk powder from a common supplier—the likely carrier of the botulism spores. Today’s powdered formula is highly industrialized, with dozens of ingredients from multiple sources. The contents of a single can of formula may contain milk from thousands of different cows. Nobody has ever fed babies this kind of stuff before. From December 2025 through February 2026, more than 100 infants in at least 10 countries were sickened in all likelihood by powdered formula tainted with spores from the bacterium Bacillus cereus. The formula, manufactured by several different companies, including Nestlé and Danone, had been contaminated by a fatty-acid additive supplied by a biotech firm in Wuhan, China.

A generation ago, an outbreak of food poisoning generally remained small-scale. The source was likely to be tainted ground beef from a local butcher shop or an egg salad gone bad at a church picnic. As the scale of industrial food production has grown, so has the scale of foodborne outbreaks. When I wrote my book Fast Food Nation, published in 2001, high levels of fecal contamination of ground beef were already a nationwide problem, not just a local one, because huge ground-beef-processing plants with poor safety procedures were supplying the fast-food industry.

The dairy industry now presents similar problems of scale. The supply chain for the botulism-tainted infant formula went like this: 55 dairies in California sold raw milk to a company called Organic West; that raw milk was then shipped from California to an enormous plant operated by Dairy Farmers of America in Fallon, Nevada, and processed into milk powder. For ByHeart, the powder was shipped to a plant in Iowa, turned into formula, shipped to Oregon for additional processing, packaged there, and sold throughout the United States. For Nara Organics, the milk powder was shipped from Nevada to Germany, manufactured into formula, shipped to Denmark, packaged, and shipped back to the U.S.

Government never adapts quickly, and because policies are adopted piecemeal over decades, many federal food-safety rules make little sense. For instance, frozen cheese pizzas are regulated by the FDA—but if a frozen pizza has a lot of pepperoni or other meats, it’s regulated by the Department of Agriculture. The U.S. is the only developed country that divides responsibility for food safety among separate government agencies. So it is hardly surprising that monitoring and enforcement have not kept up with changes in food production. The larger problem is that the food-safety system we have—underfunded for decades—is being methodically dismantled by the Trump administration.

The FDA is responsible for the safety of about 80 percent of the food consumed in the United States. Last year, James Jones, the highly respected head of the FDA’s human-foods division, resigned from his post, citing the “indiscriminate” firing of 89 staff members. The loss of such expertise threatens to cripple the agency’s food-safety efforts. Kyle Diamantas—who replaced Jones and now serves as the acting head of the FDA—has no scientific, medical, or public-health training. He is an attorney (and Donald Trump Jr.’s hunting companion). While employed at the law firm Jones Day, Diamantas defended Abbott Laboratories in a lawsuit alleging that the company had knowingly sold infant formula that could cause severe bowel problems. Abbott lost the suit and in August agreed to pay a $670 million settlement to resolve that case and other claims. In a statement to investors, Abbott said that the settlement is “not in any way an admission of liability” and that the company “remains confident in the safety of these products.”

The USDA, which has food-safety oversight of meat, eggs, and poultry, has also suffered significant cutbacks under Donald Trump, losing about one-fifth of its workforce in 2025. At the CDC, the chief food-safety expert, Daniel Jernigan, resigned in August 2025, angered by budget cuts and political interference. The number of pathogens tracked by FoodNet, a crucial CDC surveillance program, has been cut by 75 percent. The amount of money spent on FoodNet annually is a fraction of what has already been spent to renovate the Reflecting Pool in front of the Lincoln Memorial.

During the late 1890s, tainted and adulterated food was commonplace in the United States. Upton Sinclair’s muckraking 1906 novel, The Jungle, exposed a variety of noxious practices—such as making sausage from rats—and prompted President Theodore Roosevelt to support food-safety legislation. The food industry vehemently opposed Roosevelt: “We are paying all we care to pay,” one executive told Congress. The industry lost that battle—federal agencies gained regulatory power—but continues to fight back. It spends more on lobbying and political donations than the oil or defense industries do.

The tragedy is that public-health experts agree on many of the straightforward steps that should be taken to ensure food safety. And they can point to a record of success. In 2002, a year after the publication of Fast Food Nation, I met a woman named Barbara Kowalcyk, whose 2-year-old son, Kevin, had recently died after being infected with E. coli O157:H7 from a tainted hamburger.  It was an all-too-frequent occurrence back then—nationwide outbreaks of E. coli O157:H7 were routinely caused by ground beef. Kowalcyk was determined that other parents should never have to endure her experience. Trained as a biostatistician, she returned to school and earned a doctorate in environmental science and food safety. She is now a professor at George Washington University’s school of public health. A decade after we met, Kowalcyk played a leading role in campaigning for “test and hold,” a food-safety rule to prevent meat companies from shipping ground beef until it had tested negative for dangerous forms of E. coli. In 2013, the rule was finally adopted by the USDA. Few large E. coli outbreaks are today caused by ground beef.

Similar test-and-hold rules could help eliminate Salmonella from poultry. A 2022 study by Consumer Reports found that almost one-third of the ground chicken sold at American supermarkets contained Salmonella—an extraordinarily high level. Strict food-safety regulation of the poultry industry in Denmark has reduced the level of Salmonella contamination in broiler chickens there from 14 to 0.3 percent—and, as a result, the number of people sickened by Salmonella has declined by 99.6 percent. But the Trump administration recently blocked the adoption of a new rule, about to go in effect after years of deliberation at the USDA, that would have prohibited the sale of poultry products highly contaminated with Salmonella, claiming the rule would have imposed “significant financial and operational burdens on American businesses and consumers.” The Meat Institute and the National Chicken Council backed the move.

When it comes to food manufactured for infants, the federal government has enormous leverage that is going unused. The infant-formula industry is highly concentrated. Two companies, Abbott and Mead Johnson, control more than 80 percent of the market. Through the USDA’s Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children, or WIC, the federal government buys more than half of the infant formula consumed in the United States—meaning that it could swiftly mandate changes on behalf of infant health. But it hasn’t. The Republican-controlled Congress has refused to hold hearings on the botulism outbreaks or on legislation introduced in March that would expand pathogen testing of infant formula and strengthen congressional oversight. The idea of putting all federal food-safety efforts under one roof is a nonstarter.

“We are paying all we care to pay”—that was the industry response in 1906, and that is the response today. It’s the rest of us who bear the cost.

entries.title: Creating the Perfect Female Monster
entries.summary: Furious takes revenge on a fictional Jeffrey Epstein.
entries.content:
Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts

The breakout crime drama Furious opens with a scene that’s hard to watch: Catherine, a serial killer played by Lola Petticrew, is keeping a man prisoner in a row house and taunting him as he dies: “I don’t like the sounds you’re making.” The show’s creator, Liz Meriwether, is announcing right away that you will be spending time with a monster, and the discomfort amps up from there. As the show progresses, we learn that Catherine has been trafficked, and the men she is killing were involved in her abuse.

In an era when “Epstein Island” exists, Catherine represents a specific kind of psychopathic serial killer. She is, as the title suggests, one of the Furies exacting revenge in a world that hasn’t managed to execute justice for her the legal way.

Meriwether says she did not set out to make a statement on the state of female rage or American justice, or even a commentary on Epstein, yet the show may have hit a nerve because those issues are so alive right now. Nine years ago, women’s anger fueled the MeToo movement, and it seemed as if the way society confronts sexual harassment and abuse was on the brink of transformation. “Misogyny is more overt on the internet than it’s ever been,” the Atlantic staff writer Sophie Gilbert says. “And you think about what happened to that anger and what happened to that rage, and I know from my own perspective, you can’t live with that kind of anger for a decade. You just can’t. It has to burn out. It has to go somewhere, or you just get numb.”

In this episode, Meriwether talks about the complications of humanizing a serial killer and how the project of creating complicated women characters has evolved in her decade of writing for television. And Gilbert talks about what it means that more women creators are owning the stories told about women.

The following is a transcript of the episode:

Hanna Rosin: A female monster is a rare but recurring creature. She often emerges at moments in history when women in society are collectively angry at the powers that be but unable to express it. Maybe they’re too defeated or maybe numb, so the monster gets revenge for them.

I’m Hanna Rosin. This is Radio Atlantic.

Right now, there is a particularly interesting monster out there taking revenge on a fictional Jeffrey Epstein. It’s playing out on the Hulu show Furious—the season finale aired this week.

Sophie Gilbert: Well, it was one of those shows that became a slow burn, I think.

[Theme song from Furious]

Rosin: This is staff writer Sophie Gilbert.

Gilbert: When it first debuted, there wasn’t that much chatter about it. But then you started to see people watch, and it became this word-of-mouth hit.

Rosin: Furious is a dark and sometimes disturbing TV show about a female serial killer, played by Lola Petticrew, who is pursued by a female FBI agent, played by Emmy Rossum.

Gilbert: So there’s a lot about it that is quite kind of tropey, old-school procedural. It’s a crime show. The cop and the killer being pursued, they have that kind of, Oh, we’re not so different, you and I, kind of thing going on.

But at the same time, it was also like no other procedural I’ve ever seen, in the sense that in so many crime shows, you see women’s bodies used like window dressing almost. And this is a show that really seems to be made about women, not for women necessarily, but it’s interested in women. It’s interested in what happens to women when they go through traumatic experiences, what happens to women when they become angry. There’s so much that is kind of really deep and tied to these mythological elements of transformation and violence. And it just works well on so many levels.

Rosin: The show’s mythological elements are in the name. It’s called Furious after the Furies, the Greek goddesses of vengeance. In the show, the Furies are implied to be serial killer Catherine, FBI agent Alice, and Alice’s mentor, Nora—three women who, in different ways, have all failed to find the justice they need.

Gilbert: So Nora Washington is the head of the FBI’s sex-crimes unit in the show. She’s played by Quincy Tyler Bernstine in this extraordinary performance. She’s so good. And she has a few speeches where she’s talking to Alice Black, sort of the main character in the show, who’s played by Emmy Rossum, who is trying to become an FBI agent under her wing. And she’s explaining to her the toll that this job takes, of looking into these horrendous sex crimes, these crimes often against underage girls, against children.

You take on this responsibility when you do this job of doing this thing that no one else will do, to try and achieve a measure of justice, or certainly a measure of justice that is often impossible, and it changes you.

Quincy Tyler Bernstine (as Nora Washington in Furious): Everyone likes it when there’s a sweet little woman lying on the floor, naked and cut up in pieces. I get so fucking angry.

Gilbert: Because you have to become, in some ways, a monster to do this day after day.

Bernstine: It doesn’t matter, anything you do. The ones who are really to blame don’t get caught. Never. Never.

Gilbert: So there are all these sort of elemental themes of Greek tragedy and Greek drama that seem to come through.

Bernstine: You think you’re ever gonna catch anyone who matters?

Gilbert: So this show starts with a scene of a woman whose name we later find out is Catherine—she’s played by Lola Petticrew—who is keeping a man prisoner in a Brooklyn row house on Halloween.

[Sounds from Furious]

Gilbert: And Catherine is wearing a mask, and she is eating candy corn, and she is clearly torturing this man. And then eventually, we see her murder him.

Lola Petticrew (as Catherine Grace in Furious): I don’t really like listening to you. I don’t like the sounds you’re making.

Gilbert: And the show begins in this really stark way of saying, This is who this character is. Like, Be horrified by this; be appalled by her actions. It’s sort of really uncomfortable to watch in lots of ways, really visceral. And then as the show goes on, you understand more about who she is. You understand her history. You understand why she’s doing what she’s doing, her flawed but in some ways very sympathetic logic. And you see her full humanity. And she becomes, yes, a serial killer, but one who does seem to be doing it for reasons that are, if not fully justifiable, you start to sort of empathize with them a little bit more.

Rosin: Yeah. And here’s the difficult thing: The parallels to the current world are apparent. This is essentially a Jeffrey Epstein setup. It’s a setup about people who are portrayed as rich. There’s a man at the center of it. There’s a sort of a twisted luring in of teenagers and young women. It really has obvious parallels to the world we are currently living in. And here’s a woman exacting justice because the justice system wouldn’t.

Gilbert: Yes.

Rosin: So as I describe it, it is sympathetic. You are, in some ways, supposed to root for this person who at the very first scene is gruesome.

Gilbert: I don’t know if you’re supposed to root for her, but it becomes impossible not to, in some ways.

Rosin: Yeah, yeah.

Gilbert: And I think that’s part of the trick. The show is not black and white morally. It reveals things, and it explains them, and it offers context for them. And we, as human beings, watch it, and we have our own context, and we have our own life experiences, and we add. And we’re supposed to make our own judgments, but I don’t think the show is telling us what to sort of presume one way or another. And that, to me, is what makes it so interesting as an experience.

But yes, this character Jay Easton is, obviously—he’s certainly in the Jeffrey Epstein mold. He’s a billionaire. He’s revealed to have preyed on hundreds, maybe thousands of young, underage women. And yet, what again is striking about the show is that he’s not really interesting. He’s not a character who the show is sort of interested in delving into, really. The show is much more curious about the impact he’s had on the lives of women and girls, and that, I think, is often what goes underplayed or what is missing in our Epstein discourse as well. So it’s shining a light on a different facet of this very topical issue.

[Music]

Rosin: As I watched episode after episode, I had a very uncomfortable reaction that I’m guessing other people had, that the creator of the show, Liz Meriwether—who we’ll talk to later—says she intended: I was not, not rooting for the serial killer, this deeply unlikable, twisted, dark, criminal young woman who was effectively hunting down the men who had abused her when she was a teenager.

Gilbert: Without being, like, morally endorsing murder, it can be cathartic to see where they go with it and to imagine what happens when there’s no justice possible. What do you do with all that rage?

Rosin: Sophie wrote about the show recently for The Atlantic, about how the grief, anger, and rage in Furious reminded her of a different time, nearly a decade ago, when similar feelings of anger generated headlines, spawned think pieces and hashtags, and started the MeToo movement that ultimately fizzled out.

Rosin: Yeah. So what does that reflect in the culture then? A sense of frustration, helplessness? What does that mean?

Gilbert: For me, the show really resonated when I was thinking about—first of all, it’s been almost a decade since the MeToo moment, which is just wild to think about anyway, all this time. But when you think about what happened at the end of 2017, the revelations about Harvey Weinstein, the revelations about all these men—

Reporter (from ABC News): New Yorker magazine reporting new claims of sexual harassment, assault, and rape. One of his accusers going to police, secretly recording her confrontation with Weinstein, but no charges were ever filed.

Gilbert: —there was so much in the sense that we were in this moment of societal transformation and women’s anger. There were so many books written about women’s anger. There were TV shows written about women’s anger. It seemed like rage and fury, and righteous fury, was this great theme in our culture that might have a kind of revolutionary force, that it might help upend systems and overturn injustice.

Reporter (from CBS Miami): Instead of naming one person, Time magazine named its 2017 Person of the Year the “silence breakers,” the name given to the women who came forward to report sexual harassment and assault, sparking the MeToo movement.

Gilbert: And then you look nine years later and you think, Wow, actually, none of that has happened. We’ve, if anything, lost rights. Misogyny is more overt on the internet than it’s ever been. More and more injustices and horrific crimes against women and girls are revealed. I mean, really, it feels almost daily. We have an overtly misogynist president, I would say. And you think about what happened to that anger and what happened to that rage, and I know from my own perspective, you can’t live with that kind of anger for a decade. You just can’t. It has to burn out. It has to go somewhere, or you just get numb, I think.

And so what this show is doing, which really connected with my own sense of just being unable to feel that rage day after day after day, is wondering what happens when it becomes something else, when it takes a different direction, when it realizes that justice is impossible, and so vengeance is the next best thing.

Rosin: Hmm.

I wanna ask about the broad sweep of things. In your book, Girl on Girl, the thesis is that pop culture taught Millennial women to hate themselves, or maybe just that pop culture of the ’90s and aughts hated women in a certain way. This is a show conceived of by women, written by women, in which a woman and the Furies do get revenge. Does that at least agency, even if it’s a perverse agency, does that represent something different, like controlling the narrative?

Gilbert: Yes, the stories that we get now about women, about the complexities of their lives, the conditions that they’re living under, like the truth of their experience, are made by women about women.

There’s so much that is so much better than it was even 10 years ago.
