And I was reading an interview with Liz Meriwether, the creator of Furious, where she said—because she’s the creator of a much-beloved sitcom, one of my favorites, called New Girl—and she was mentioning the notes that she got from Fox in terms of sort of making the character more likable and making it broadly more appealing to men, and how now, making this show, Furious, there was none of that.

There’s much more appetite I think, or at least more understanding on the part of people commissioning work like this, that you can be interested in women as a subject and that will make great art that will connect with viewers and be enough of a justification. We don’t need to always be kind of shushing women in a way.

Rosin: Yeah. And it’s not just, you can be interested in women. You can be interested—I mean, the task she’s setting out for a viewer here is: You can be interested in a woman who’s, like you said, a monster. From the very first scene, she’s the exact opposite of a beautiful dead victim. She couldn’t be less likable, at least in the very beginning.

Gilbert: Yes. And the show really trusts us as audiences to see that and to keep watching, which I think is fascinating all on its own. Like, there’s this idea that we don’t need to be coddled into finding this woman cute and sexy. (Laughs.)

Rosin: Yeah.

Gilbert: We can see what she is and we can be hooked anyway, because we’re sophisticated enough consumers of media to understand that the payoff might be worth it.

[Music]

Rosin: After the break, we talk to the Furious showrunner, Liz Meriwether, about why she created a monster you don’t necessarily hate.

[Break]

[Music]

Rosin: Liz Meriwether started as a comedy writer. As Sophie mentioned, her breakout hit was New Girl. Then she wrote The Dropout, a show about Theranos founder and convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes—also not a classic lovable type. And then Dying for Sex, about a woman who has a terminal-cancer diagnosis—so potentially a perfect victim—but instead, she decides to spend her final months having a lot of sex.

We’ve talked a lot on this episode about post-MeToo progress being stalled. But this—this creation, by female writers, of female characters who test the bounds of likability—is also a kind of progress. I talk to Meriwether—who is in the writers’ room working on Season 2 of Furious—about how her ability to write female characters exactly how she wants them has evolved.

[Music]

Rosin: So the terrible word that’s imposed on female characters forever, which is likable—female politicians, everybody, likability. From the very first scene, you make the decision to make Catherine not likable. Did you get any pushback on that? Like, Put some woman in there who is more pure, or a sort of more recognizable person you can attach yourself to?

Meriwether: As somebody who’s been doing this for about 15 years now, and when I first started doing it, got that note all the time, I was surprised that I didn’t get that note.

Rosin: Can you actually talk about that? ’Cause you were mostly known as a comedy writer. New Girl was the breakout hit, and when you were writing that, what were the conversations like about how weird or unconventional a main character who’s a woman could be?

Meriwether: Yeah. The notes I got were, like—the first pilot I wrote was called Sluts. It was kind of Girls before Girls, in a way. It was three girls in New York who just, like, had a lot of sex and just were deciding to get their lives together and sort of stop having so much sex. And this was for Fox. It was never gonna get on the air. But that was the first pilot that I wrote, and I had conversations with executives that were like, She either is smart, or she likes sex, and that was a binary thing that I had to genuinely have a conversation with somebody about, where I was like, No, you can be smart and also have had a lot of sex.

Rosin: So you were in your 20s when you wrote that pilot, when you wrote Sluts.

Meriwether: Yeah, I was, like, 25 or something. Yeah.

Rosin: And did you already know, I’m trying to push against some kind of tropes or ideas of how female characters should be?

Meriwether: Yeah. I mean, I think I’ve always come from a place of, like, I’m gonna make jokes about it or try to come at it from a little bit of a sneakier place. I’ve never been a writer that’s been very I have a big statement I wanna make. Which is, honestly, why this show kinda scared me a little bit, because I was like, I don’t get to hide as much.

I don’t get to kind of, like, you know, tap-dance and make jokes and say, like, No, look over here. Look over here. Look over here. But yes, I’ve always been interested in trying to put women on screen that are not what you have seen before. That’s been something that I’ve been interested in for a long time.

I just feel like we’ve taken steps forward and steps back over the past 15 years, but there’s definitely more complicated female characters on television now than there was back then.

When New Girl first aired, I did a lot of press. It was, like, me and Whitney Cummings had comedies coming out, and [people] were like, We can’t believe there are, like, comedies written by women—more than one comedy written by women.

That was like the main thrust of the press. And that would never be a story nowadays. So yes, there, I mean, there is growth. I think that there’s also a lot of moving forward then moving backwards.

Rosin: Yeah. For this episode, we also interviewed my Atlantic colleague Sophie Gilbert, who wrote this book Girl on Girl, which is about how pop culture of the late ’90s and aughts hated women or taught Millennial women to hate themselves.

And I was thinking about you because you, that’s your era of pop culture. I also saw that you signed on to write the biopic of Britney Spears, who is the ultimate example of how the late ’90s and early aughts chewed some women up. And so I wondered if that was part of what motivates you or what excites you about these kinds of projects.

Meriwether: I think so. Yeah. I mean, I do kinda just keep my head down and keep moving forward. Like, I don’t go from a place of like I have an agenda. But yes, those are the characters that really excite me—the women where it’s, like, very hard to put into words how you feel about them. You don’t know if you’re rooting for them or not. I do think it’s a very interesting, fun place to be as a writer, maybe because of all of the notes I got about likability and the desire to sort of get away from that. But I also think it’s not interesting to make somebody completely evil. I think that middle space is really interesting.

Rosin: And maybe it just feels more true.

Meriwether: Yeah. There’s also a tendency to, say, victimize women in a different way, where it’s like they had no agency in what happened to them or, you know, they are completely products of a broken system, which I feel like is not fair either and a little bit patronizing and boring, honestly. So I think I’m interested in, like, all the nuances of why people do the things they do.

[Music]

Rosin: Sophie, you know what I was thinking about? The Olivia Rodrigo reprisal of Lilith Fair.

Olivia Rodrigo: 45,000 people at this festival tonight. Can you believe it?

Rosin: I don’t know if you saw the documentary about Lilith Fair.

Gilbert: I did, yeah.

Rosin: So I watched that documentary, and I think I might have cried, honestly, because I thought, Oh, well, that era is dead. Like, We will never, ever have that back again.

[Sounds from the Lilith Fair: Building a Mystery trailer]

Rosin: A sort of collection of women getting together, talking about their music, entirely made for and run by women, and yet here it is reprised this summer. And I thought, Oh, maybe the sense of agency that’s emerging, it does feel different than what you wrote about [in your book]. It does feel different than the Britney Spears era, the era in which women died by those cultural stories. Now it feels like they’re writing the stories, and so even though they might be grim or they might be inspirational, they are controlling the narrative.

Gilbert: That Lilith documentary was so good and I think so sad, for exactly the reasons that you said, which was: It seemed the last moment when this idea of a women-centric society, or at least an alternative society, seemed possible. (Laughs.) And then everything that happened afterwards in the 2000s, and just this real decade of victimizing women for living their lives in public.

But yes, again, we have this moment of a mainstream pop star holding a massive music festival for abortion-rights charities and reproductive rights, which you can’t imagine someone like Taylor Swift doing that.

Rodrigo: Today I’m so aware of all the women who came before me, who fought for me to enjoy the rights that I enjoy today.

Gilbert: All right, it’s not as subversive and as edgy as what riot-grrrl musicians were doing in the ’90s, but it’s political. It’s active. It’s angry about the way that things are, and it’s willing to take a stand to change them. And then it also—I think the thing that I found so fascinating about this festival, Daisy Chain, was that it just demonstrates the power that women have in the music industry.

Of all the different cultural industries, music really seems to be one where women are dominant right now—where they sell the most records, where they’re making the most interesting music, where they’re the ones that we are drawn to. They have these huge tours, and they have this huge fandom, and they are front and center in music and powerful in a way that men are not. And that, I think, is interesting right now, in this moment. And the question of why, I don’t know. But if we’re looking for things to be hopeful about, that’s definitely one.

Rosin: Right, ’cause in thinking about women’s anger, I got stuck in a kind of limited narrative, which is, Oh, in 2017, women were able to channel the anger in a productive direction. People told their stories. Sort of a dam burst open. There were truths out there, and that was cathartic. And in 2026, we get a serial killer. So then I was trying to think, Well, maybe that’s not that simple. There are places that anger finds an out that are more joyful or productive, and so this is one that I look to.

Gilbert: Yeah. Olivia Rodrigo just released a song called “Serena Joy,” which is named, obviously, after the character in The Handmaid’s Tale who has helped subjugate other women. One of the lyrics in it is, “If you can’t throw a punch, you can learn how to spit.”

[“Serena Joy,” by Olivia Rodrigo]

Gilbert: Just, it’s this idea that numbness is not inevitable. We don’t have to just be complacent forever and ever and ever while our rights are eroded and things are taken away—that in some ways, cultural power is still there, and that there are still women sort of taking a stand for things, and in some ways, storytelling is able to do such interesting work now because we are in a different place than we were in 2017, and we’re much more open to ideas about what’s possible, even if it doesn’t seem like it’s easily achievable.

Rosin: Yeah. Well, Sophie, thank you so much for talking this through with me today.

Gilbert: Oh, it’s a pleasure. Thank you for having me.

[Music]

Rosin: This episode of Radio Atlantic was produced by Rosie Hughes and Jinae West with help from Jacob Smollen. It was edited by Claudine Ebeid. Rob Smierciak engineered and provided original music. We also had music from Breakmaster Cylinder. Fact-checking by Sam Fentress. Claudine Ebeid is the executive producer of Atlantic audio, and Andrea Valdez is our managing editor.

Listeners, if you enjoy the show, you can support our work and the work of all Atlantic journalists when you subscribe to The Atlantic at TheAtlantic.com/Listener.

I’m Hanna Rosin. Thank you for listening.

entries.title: How ‘Somatics’ Became the Solution to Modern Life
entries.summary: The word isn’t new—but lately, it’s everywhere.
entries.content:
The word isn’t new—but lately, it’s everywhere.

When clients go to Sybil Ottenstein for therapy, they tend to arrive with answers. Many of them have seen shrinks before. They can tell her which events from their past were formative, and point to the ripple effects in their current life. They’re like detectives, she told me, with all the dots connected on their corkboard of evidence. Intellectually, they’ve cracked the case. The problem is that they don’t feel any better.

That’s why they’re seeking something different from Ottenstein: somatic psychotherapy. Traditional talk therapy could be seen as a top-down approach. You identify problems in your thinking, your habits, or your life, and hope that by working through them, you can resolve physical manifestations of emotional issues—the chest palpitations of anxiety, the stomachache of stress. Somatic therapy, by contrast, works from the bottom up. Ottenstein typically starts her sessions by asking clients to slow down and pay attention to corporeal sensations: “What does it feel like in your chest? In your throat?” As they talk, she encourages them to stay in their body, to let themselves feel whatever is coming up. People cry. They yawn. They scream. They stretch. They dance.

The word somatic, according to Merriam-Webster, merely means “of, relating to, or affecting the body.” But recently, it’s been popping up everywhere, appended to a variety of practices that involve tuning in to physical symptoms in order to ameliorate psychological ones. Somatic therapists like Ottenstein have noticed a significant bump in interest; one of the major somatic-therapy training programs reported that its applicants more than doubled from 2020 to 2023. Other practitioners offer somatic dance, somatic yoga, somatic workouts. (The terms seem a touch redundant.)

On Instagram, hundreds of thousands of posts appear with the hashtag #somatic. A “somatic exercise” trainer who goes by the “Workout Witch” (nearly 2 million followers) teaches small, repetitive movements meant to discharge negative feelings—curl your head down for “sorrow/despair,” pull your right ear for “overwhelm”—and promises that “trauma can be released from your hips.” All over my feed, fit young women are humming, hitting their sternum, pinching their nose bridge, and bouncing their knees all the way to inner peace.

Much of the time, as with many other wellness ventures, someone stands to make money. At one somatic-workout class I attended, where a staffer told me that the goal was to “move stagnant energy out,” the lobby featured a gift-shop corner with jewelry, T-shirts, and $65 “body gloss” from a brand called Oui the People. But clearly, plenty of Americans are willing to pay for the promise of a psychic cleanse. Practitioners refer to “stuck energy,” to “trapped emotions,” to “resetting” a nervous system caught in fight-or-flight mode. “We have all these ways of just storing that gunk inside,” Ottenstein told me. I pictured, uncomfortably, a thick, black goo running through my veins.

Somatics—the whole roomy umbrella of practices—might seem like an odd fit for the information age, when people are more accustomed to finding answers on the internet than within themselves. But that could be precisely the draw for thinkers and analyzers who are tired of ruminating in anxious circles, who spend their days in front of a laptop and nights scrolling an iPhone. For millennia, people have yearned to break out of the confines of their bodies; they’ve searched—through religion, spirituality, drugs—for transcendence. Now, for some, the existential quest is inverted: Instead of seeking to escape their prison of flesh and bones, they want to reinhabit it.

The origin of somatics is difficult to pinpoint, though it’s certainly not recent. Some credit Wilhelm Reich, a student of Freud’s, who theorized in the early 1900s that patients held tension in their bodies—“muscular armor”—as a subconscious defense against trauma, leading to aches, pains, and inflammation. But it wasn’t until the 1970s that the field began to formalize, developed in part by the American philosophy professor Thomas Hanna, who defined somatics as the study of “the body as perceived from within.” That same decade, a UC Berkeley biophysics doctoral student, Peter Levine, developed “somatic experiencing”: a therapeutic method based on the idea that people, like other animals, react to trauma with a flight, fight, or freeze response, powered by a burst of adrenaline. After the source of danger is gone, Levine argued, they have pent-up “survival energy” to unleash: They need to physically shake it off. He pointed to videos of impalas, quaking and buckling after surviving a cheetah attack. When humans go through something upsetting, Ottenstein told me, “we go to work the next day.”

This idea—that trauma is held in the body, and thus must be physically remedied—was once fairly niche. In recent years, though, it has been jolted into prominence. The psychiatrist Bessel van der Kolk’s book The Body Keeps the Score, which argues for somatic treatments of PTSD, was first released in 2014 and was not an immediate hit. In 2021, it reached the No. 1 spot on the New York Times best-seller list for paperback nonfiction. And although it has been accused of resting on shaky science, it has continued to dominate the charts for years.

Van der Kolk wrote about violent assaults, wartime atrocities, severe childhood abuse—circumstances that many readers hadn’t directly experienced. Yet The Body Keeps the Score seemed to resonate anyway. When it gained momentum, lots of Americans had spent the previous year safe in their homes, baking bread and taking Zoom calls. (“When people say the pandemic has been a collective trauma,” van der Kolk told The Atlantic that year, “I say, absolutely not.”) Most had also, however, been detached from the rich sensory experience of interacting with the external world. Now here was a book about people who’d felt estranged from their own body—and then, through simple movement, play, and touch, found their way back to their surroundings, and to themselves.

In the years since, most people have emerged from pandemic isolation. Yet the share of Americans who say they frequently experience stress, which has been rising for decades, has continued its upward trend. Talk therapy remains popular, but it’s not always affordable or accessible—and much of the time, it doesn’t take physical symptoms into account. Meanwhile, many medical doctors don’t consider psychological causes of physical ailments. Stress in particular is “like this mythical creature,” Aditi Nerurkar, a physician at Harvard Medical School, told me. “And we don’t have a lot of time. We have to focus on your hemoglobin. Did you get a mammogram? Did you get a pap smear? What is your cholesterol?”

No wonder, then, that somatics is a flourishing industry. Many Americans already distrust medical institutions; maybe they want to bypass the dismissive doctor, or the therapist who wants to rehash every daddy issue but can’t seem to fix anything. So they turn to this strange constellation of New Age–y courses, TikTok sages, and licensed counselors. Some offerings target people with capital-T Trauma; others claim to be for just about anyone. Many present themselves as alternatives to more traditional paths to mental well-being. The question is whether they can really help the frazzled masses.

Somatics does get a lot of things right. Plenty of bodily sensations are, at root, psychological. Some communication does need to happen between the brain and the rest of the body. That’s how you know to respond to danger: The amygdala triggers the nervous system to increase your heart rate, deliver more blood to muscles, and release a flood of adrenaline. When I spoke with Nerurkar, she rattled off an incomplete list of physical symptoms that might result from stress: headaches, dizziness, nausea, vision changes. When she was in residency training, she said, she experienced what felt like a “stampede of wild horses” across her chest and was convinced that she had a heart problem—until her doctors, having conducted a battery of tests, recommended that she seriously consider chilling out.

And many components of somatic practice have evidence to back them up. Interoception, or awareness of one’s own physical signals, really can be important for well-being—perhaps because it increases people’s sense of attunement with their body, connection with the present moment, or agency over otherwise vague and inscrutable sensations. Mindfulness meditation, which involves interoception, has been shown to decrease stress and anxiety and even reduce physical pain. Yoga and breathing exercises can decrease amygdala activation and lead to better concentration, memory, and executive function.

But the somatics packaging of these techniques is alluring partly because of the emotional liberation it promises. Somaticists tend to describe a clear path: identify a physical signal, connect it to its psychic cause, then let it go. If the nervous system overactivates, surely you can just reset it. If the body holds trauma, surely the body can relinquish it.

These were always just metaphors, though, and imperfect ones. The amygdala doesn’t have a reboot button. There is no viscous gunk of emotional pain to flush out. The Body Keeps the Score has been somewhat debunked; critics have argued that van der Kolk incorrectly described certain studies, and that he seems to have made up others entirely. (Responding to the writer Emi Nietfeld’s critique in Mother Jones, van der Kolk said that at times he drew on unpublished data.) Trauma experts have pushed back on his wholesale condemnation of talk therapy, which can be, according to a mountain of evidence, very helpful for treating PTSD. There’s also something ironic in how certain somaticists—ostensibly advocates for the mind-body connection—talk as if the two are separated by a nearly unbridgeable gap: the physical burden of trauma unreachable through thinking or conversation, and perhaps not even accessible to conscious awareness.

So somatics isn’t a miracle cure. And it’s probably right to be skeptical of influencers who seek to collect on people’s need to feel at home in their body. But that doesn’t mean somatics can’t be helpful. Much of it, after all, turns out to be pretty straightforward. Movement is good, generally. Breathing is good. Stepping away from your screen—stretching your limbs, remembering you are real and tangible and mortal—is good.

When I signed up for that somatic-exercise class, I expected that I might leave rolling my eyes, but I secretly hoped I’d walk out lighter, more alive and connected to myself and the world. What I found was something in between. The actual workout couldn’t have been more basic: It consisted largely of squats, jumping jacks, crunches, some yoga—downward dog, child’s pose. Occasionally the instructor would remind us to check in with our bodies: “What are you being invited into? And I don’t mean the burpee.” Or: “Let the chin enter the conversation.” Otherwise it hardly seemed uniquely somatic, or uniquely anything.

Then again, I had the post-workout endorphin glow. I’d left my apartment and shut my phone in a locker. An hour later, I exited the studio somewhat baffled. But walking out onto a busy Manhattan street, I felt a little more conscious of the sun on my cheek, the solidness of the ground pushing against my feet. This was silly, I thought. And also: Maybe I’ll come back.
